one_liner: Portable table-driven CRC-32 (zlib polynomial) in C++. Slicing-by-8/16 runs about 3.7-8.5x faster than a byte-wise Sarwate loop.
what_it_does: A small C++ library (Crc32.h + Crc32.cpp) that computes the standard CRC-32 used by zlib, gzip, PNG and Ethernet (reflected polynomial 0xEDB88320, pre/post inversion). It ships a menu of software algorithms: bitwise, branch-free, half-byte, table-less byte, Sarwate, slicing-by-4/8/16, and slicing-by-16 with prefetch. crc32_fast() picks the largest one enabled. Every function has the shape crc32_xxx(const void* data, size_t length, uint32_t previousCrc32 = 0), so running and chunked CRCs chain. crc32_combine() merges two CRCs for parallel or chunked computation. The code is mirrored from the author's long blog post, which explains each algorithm.
how_it_is_fast: Slicing-by-N (Intel's slicing-by-8 generalized to 16 by Bulat Ziganshin) replaces Sarwate's one serial table lookup per byte with N independent lookups into N precomputed 256-entry tables per 4/8/16-byte word. That breaks the byte-to-byte dependency chain, so the CPU can issue the loads in parallel: about 1-1.5 cycles/byte vs about 8 for Sarwate on a Core i7 860. The slicing-by-16 loop is unrolled 4x, and a variant issues __builtin_prefetch/_mm_prefetch 256 bytes ahead, which the page credits with a little under 10% on that CPU. The tables are compile-time constants (up to 16 KB), so there is no runtime initialization.
when_to_use: Portable software CRC-32 (zlib/PNG/gzip-compatible) with no intrinsics, assembler or SIMD, on any ISA including big-endian, when PCLMULQDQ/ARMv8-CRC code paths are unavailable or not allowed

Embedded or memory-tight targets where you trade table size for speed: half-byte needs 64 bytes of table, Sarwate 1 KB, slicing-by-4/8/16 4/8/16 KB; there are Arduino sketches and blog cycle counts for the ATmega
Replacing a hand-rolled byte-wise CRC loop in legacy C++: slicing-by-16 was about 8x faster on a 2010-era x86 desktop (375 MB/s to 3,000 MB/s with GCC 4.7)
Chunked or multi-threaded CRC of large buffers, using crc32_combine() to merge per-chunk CRCs (the repo includes a std::thread example)
Learning or teaching CRC implementation tradeoffs: the blog documents each algorithm step by step with code and measurements
when_not_to_use: Modern x86-64 or ARMv8 servers and desktops: carry-less-multiply or hardware CRC libraries (crc32fast pclmulqdq, corsix fast-crc32, zlib-ng, Chromium zlib) run many times faster, and this library has no hardware path at all

As a claimed upgrade over zlib's crc32(): zlib has used a four-bytes-at-a-time (BYFOUR) loop since 1.2.0 (2003) and braided CRC since 1.2.12 (2022, '1.5 to 3' times faster per its ChangeLog). The page's 'zlib' baseline is really a Sarwate loop, and no comparison against actual zlib exists
CRC-32C (Castagnoli, iSCSI/ext4/SSE4.2) or any other polynomial: the tables are hard-coded for 0xEDB88320

Small-core ARM without verification: a user's Raspberry Pi 2 (ARMv7) run in issue #16 measured 101 MB/s for Sarwate vs only 172-218 MB/s for the slicing variants (about 1.7-2.2x), and slicing-by-16 without prefetch was slower than slicing-by-8 there
Projects that need an actively maintained dependency: no commits since 2021-09-29, and seven issues/PRs are open without response, including build and portability fixes

integration.dependencies: none (stdint.h, cstddef; sys/param.h on non-Windows for __BYTE_ORDER; xmmintrin.h for prefetch under MSVC with SSE2)
integration.min_toolchain: Any C++ compiler for the library, which uses no C++11 features in Crc32.cpp (default arguments and <cstddef> make it C++-only). Measured with GCC 4.7 and Visual C++ 2010; the multithreaded test needs C++11 (std::thread, auto)
integration.platforms: any; little- and big-endian paths for slicing-by-4/8/16; Windows ARM64 fixed in 2021; Arduino sketch ports; no SIMD or hardware-CRC path on any architecture
integration.thread_safety: Not documented explicitly; all functions are pure and the lookup tables are static const, so concurrent calls are safe. The README advertises multi-threaded computation via crc32_combine()
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — produces the same CRC-32 values as zlib's crc32() and a byte-wise Sarwate loop, and chains through previousCrc32, but argument order differs (data, length, previousCrc vs zlib's crc, buf, len) and the header has no extern "C" (the PR adding it was closed unmerged)

gotchas: The slicing functions cast the void* input straight to const uint32_t* with no alignment prologue. Misaligned buffers (for example from chunked processing) rely on the CPU tolerating unaligned loads, which is UB in C++ and can fault on strict-alignment cores; the author only warns that 'performance might suffer'
Non-Windows builds need __BYTE_ORDER from <sys/param.h> or stop with #error; an open 2022 PR reports macOS failing this way and proposes falling back to __BYTE_ORDER__
Crc32.h itself #defines all four CRC32_USE_LOOKUP_TABLE_* switches, so shrinking the 16 KB table for embedded use means editing the header, not passing -U flags

crc32_combine() uses the older pigz/zlib GF(2) matrix-squaring method on every call; zlib 1.2.12 made combines about 200x faster with precomputed tables. The bundled Crc32Test allocates 1 GiB and throws std::bad_alloc on 32-bit boards (issue #16)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over crc32fast, corsix fast-crc32, komrad36/CRC or the dougallj PMULL kernel only when you need plain portable C++ with no SIMD or hardware dependency, or a tiny-table variant for microcontrollers. Chorba is the newer table-less software alternative that beats zlib's braided CRC. htot/crc32c computes the different CRC-32C polynomial.
verified_claims_summary: The author's blog table times CRC-32 over a 1 GiB buffer on a Core i7 860 (2.8/3.2 GHz) with GCC 4.7 and Visual C++ 2010 (exact flags not stated): 1,800/1,400 MB/s for slicing-by-8, 3,000/2,000 for slicing-by-16 and 3,200/2,000 with prefetch. The reference is his own byte-wise Sarwate loop at 375 MB/s, about 3.7-8.5x (derived). zlib's actual crc32() was never benchmarked.
status_note: Abandoned (last commit 2021-09-29, open PRs unanswered). The code is Zlib-licensed, two files, dependency-free and trivially vendorable, but it predates hardware-accelerated CRC and was last tuned for 2010-2015 compilers and CPUs.
